## Goals

1. Understand the importance of discussing technical issues on programming projects.
2. Practice setting up a repository with a team.
3. Practice doing a code review.

## Before Class

A team developing software often has individuals contributing features, tests, and other changes to a repository.
In the Git/GitHub-like universe, this manifests as proposing *pull requests*.
A pull request is a series changes, packaged as Git commits, that individuals wish to incorporate into a codebase.
The practice of *code review* aims to systematically review such requests to check for (not exhaustive):

- consistency in style, particularly with respect to the rest of the codebase,
- potential bugs or flaws in design,
- readability, and
- tests for important scenarios or edge cases.

Adhering to a consistent code review approach should, in theory, improve code quality and build a shared sense of ownership and responsibility amongst a team.
In this lab, you will practice code (peer) review on one of your assignments.

- Read GitHub's reference manual on [pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/pull-requests). Don't worry about the other items on the left hand side menu.
- Make contact with your final project team members.
- Accept the invitation to your team on GitHub.

## Instructions

1. Pair up in your teams for the Final Project.
2. Create a new repository for this assignment.
    + Designate one team member to create a repository within the UCR-STAT-206 organization.
    + That individual should invite everyone else to the repository; navigate to Settings > Collaborators > Manage Access > Add People.
3. Add files for code review.
    + Using the GitHub web interface, each member should create a separate directory and upload their **committed files** for Homework 3.
    + Make sure directories have distinct names.
4. Commit the new files.
    + Using the GitHub web interface, create a commit as a pull request/separate branch. That is, make sure you select "Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request".
5. Write the commit message.
    + Include a descriptive message as part of the commit.
    + *Examples*: What files are being added, why are you adding them, are there any details a reviewer should be aware of.
6. Now each team member will go to the pull request made by another team member and look at the code changes.
7. Read each other's code carefully and leave some thoughtful comments.
    + Comments can be about organization, filenames, formatting (in code or the Quarto document), readability, or issues with reproducibility.
    + It is possible to be both constructive and kind.

## Additional Tasks

1. Time permitting, discuss your approach to implementing `nnmf()`.
2. Time permitting, try downloading someone else's work to your container and run `quarto render somefile.qmd` on one of their assignments.

## Some Questions to Guide Reviews

- How is the code organized? Is it organized?
- Are there absolute or relative file paths?
- Is there a `Project.toml` recording the project's dependencies?
- Are packages loaded up front or scattered throughout the main report?
- Does the author explain their implementation or otherwise document the approach taken to the main implementation?
- Is it easy to read the report?
- Are there any tests, checks, or assertions? Any that should be implemented?
